transcript.text: My Panasonic NN-ST45KWBPQ is sparking inside when I heat soup, little blue flashes on the right-hand wall and a crackling noise. I stopped it. Is it safe?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using the microwave now: switch it off at the socket and unplug it, and don't run it again (not even empty) until we know why it sparked. Never take the outer casing off — parts inside can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged. No — do not use it again, even briefly, until it has been checked by a qualified microwave engineer. Blue flashes and crackling are internal arcing, not normal operation. Because it was flashing from the right-hand wall, the leading possibility is the waveguide cover: a small flat mica panel inside the cavity which can arc if food/grease has burnt onto it or it is damaged. Metal or foil in the cavity, chipped cavity paint, and less commonly an internal high-voltage fault can also cause this. 1. With it switched off, unplugged and cool, remove the glass tray and look inside only — do not remove the outer casing or any internal cover.
2. Check for any foil, metal, twist-ties, or dishes with metallic trim. Also inspect the small flat panel on the right-hand wall and the surrounding paint. - Blackening, a burn mark, hole, or chipped paint supports a cavity/waveguide fault. - Food splatter or grease may explain where the arcing began, but it still needs professional assessment before the microwave is used.
3. Do not run a cup-of-water test or try it again to see whether it clears. If you can describe what that right-hand panel looks like, and whether anything metallic was in with the soup, I can tell you which cause is most likely — but either way, this needs an engineer before further use.

No metal, it was just soup in a plain plastic bowl. The panel on the right wall looks a bit like cardboard, with a black burnt spot and greasy splatter on it. There was a slight burnt smell and one wisp of smoke from that spot, which stopped when I switched it off.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. No — it must not be used again until a qualified microwave engineer has checked it. The blackened, greasy cardboard-like panel is very likely the waveguide cover (mica cover). The arcing, burnt smell and small amount of smoke point to food/grease contamination having carbonised on that cover, or to the cover itself being burnt through. A damaged cavity coating behind or beside it is the other important possibility. Do not switch it back on to test it, and do not remove or replace that panel yourself. An engineer needs to inspect the cover and the metal cavity/waveguide area behind it, then deal with any carbon tracking or coating damage as well as the cover. If the paint around it is chipped, rusty or bare metal is visible, tell the engineer that too.

candidates: Damaged or food-contaminated waveguide (mica) cover on the right-hand wall (high)
Metal, foil or metallic decoration in the cavity (medium)
Burnt/chipped cavity coating or an internal high-voltage fault (low)

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit.
